{{Short description|Movement of entangled polymer chains}}
{{distinguish|reputation}}
{{For|the process of sediment transport by wind|Aeolian processes}}

'''Reptation''' is the [[thermal motion]] of very long linear [[macromolecules]] in  ''entangled'' [[polymer]] melts or concentrated polymer solutions.<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Pokrovskii |first1=V. N. |title=The Mesoscopic Theory of Polymer Dynamics |doi=10.1007/978-90-481-2231-8 |series=Springer Series in Chemical Physics |volume=95 |year=2010 |bibcode=2010mtpd.book.....P |isbn=978-90-481-2230-1}}</ref> Derived from the word [[reptile]], reptation suggests the movement of entangled polymer chains as being analogous to [[snake]]s slithering through one another.<ref name="Rubinstein">{{cite conference|url=http://www.aps.org/units/dpoly/resources/degennes.cfm |title=Dynamics of Entangled Polymers |publisher=American Physical Society |access-date=6 April 2015 |author=Rubinstein, Michael |date=March 2008 |conference=Pierre-Gilles de Gennes Symposium |location=New Orleans, LA}}</ref> [[Pierre-Gilles de Gennes]] introduced (and named) the concept of reptation into polymer physics in 1971 to explain the dependence of the mobility of a macromolecule on its length. Reptation is used as a mechanism to explain viscous flow in an amorphous polymer.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=De Gennes |first1=P. G. |title=Entangled polymers |doi=10.1063/1.2915700 |journal=Physics Today |volume=36 |issue=6 |page=33|year=1983 |quote=A theory based on the snake-like motion by which chains of monomers move in the melt is enhancing our understanding of rheology, diffusion, polymer-polymer welding, chemical kinetics and biotechnology|bibcode=1983PhT....36f..33D }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=De Gennes |first1=P. G. |title=Reptation of a Polymer Chain in the Presence of Fixed Obstacles |doi=10.1063/1.1675789 |journal=The Journal of Chemical Physics |volume=55 |issue=2 |page=572|year=1971 |bibcode=1971JChPh..55..572D}}</ref> [[Sam Edwards (physicist)|Sam Edwards]] and [[Masao Doi]] later refined reptation theory.<ref>{{citation|title=Samuel Edwards: Boltzmann Medallist 1995 |publisher=IUPAP Commission on Statistical Physics |url=http://iupap.cii.fc.ul.pt/Boltz_Award/BA1995.html |access-date=2013-02-20 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131017061732/http://iupap.cii.fc.ul.pt/Boltz_Award/BA1995.html |archive-date=2013-10-17 }}</ref><ref name="flow">{{Cite journal |last1=Doi |first1=M. |last2=Edwards |first2=S. F. |doi=10.1039/f29787401789 |title=Dynamics of concentrated polymer systems. Part 1.?Brownian motion in the equilibrium state |journal=Journal of the Chemical Society, Faraday Transactions 2 |volume=74 |pages=1789–1801 |year=1978}}</ref> 

[[File:Reptation.svg|thumb|250px|Reptation—motion of long linear, entangled macromolecules amorphous polymers.]]

Two closely related concepts are '''reptons''' and '''entanglement'''. A repton is a mobile point residing in the cells of a lattice, connected by bonds.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Barkema |first1=G. T. |last2=Panja |first2=D. |last3=Van Leeuwen |first3=J. M. J. |author-link3=Hans van Leeuwen (physicist)
|doi=10.1063/1.3580287 |title=Structural modes of a polymer in the repton model |journal=The Journal of Chemical Physics |volume=134 |issue=15 |page=154901 |year=2011 |pmid= 21513412 |arxiv=1102.1394 |bibcode=2011JChPh.134o4901B|s2cid=1979411 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Rubinstein |first1=M. |title=Discretized model of entangled-polymer dynamics |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.59.1946 |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=59 |issue=17 |pages=1946–1949 |year=1987 |pmid=10035375 |bibcode=1987PhRvL..59.1946R}}</ref> Entanglement means the topological restriction of molecular motion by other chains.<ref>{{Cite journal|doi=10.1080/00018730210153216|title=Tube theory of entangled polymer dynamics|journal=Advances in Physics|volume=51|issue=6|pages=1379–1527|year=2002|last1=McLeish |first1=T. C. B. |bibcode=2002AdPhy..51.1379M |author-link1= Tom McLeish |s2cid=122657744 }}</ref>

== Theory and mechanism ==

'''Reptation theory''' describes the effect of [[polymer]] chain entanglements on the relationship between [[molecular mass]] and chain [[Relaxation (physics)|relaxation time]]. The theory predicts that, in entangled systems, the relaxation time {{math|''τ''}} is proportional to the cube of molecular mass, {{math| ''M''}}: {{math| ''τ'' ∝ ''M''<sup> 3</sup>}}. The prediction of the theory can be arrived at by a relatively simple argument. First, each polymer chain is envisioned as occupying a tube of length {{math | ''L''}}, through which it may move with snake-like motion (creating new sections of tube as it moves). Furthermore, if we consider a time scale comparable to {{math |''τ''}}, we may focus on the overall, global motion of the chain. Thus, we define the tube mobility as
: {{math | ''μ''<sub>tube</sub> {{=}} ''v'' / ''f''}},
where {{math| ''v''}} is the [[velocity]] of the chain when it is pulled by a [[force]], {{math| ''f''}}. {{math| ''μ''<sub>tube</sub>}} will be [[Proportionality (mathematics)#Inverse proportionality|inversely proportional]] to the [[degree of polymerization]] (and thus also inversely proportional to chain weight).

The [[Mass diffusivity|diffusivity]] of the chain through the tube may then be written as
: {{math| ''D''<sub>tube</sub> {{=}} ''k''<sub>B</sub> ''T'' ''μ''<sub>tube</sub>}}.
By then recalling that in 1-dimension the [[mean squared displacement]] due to [[Brownian motion]] is given by
: {{math|s(''t'')<sup>2</sup> {{=}} 2''D''<sub>tube</sub> ''t''}},
we obtain
: {{math|s(''t'')<sup>2</sup> {{=}} 2''k''<sub>B</sub> ''T'' ''μ''<sub>tube</sub> ''t''}}.
The time necessary for a polymer chain to displace the length of its original tube is then
: {{math|''t'' {{=}} ''L''<sup>2</sup> / (2''k''<sub>B</sub> ''T'' ''μ''<sub>tube</sub>)}}. 
By noting that this time is comparable to the relaxation time, we establish that {{math|''τ'' ∝ ''L''<sup>2</sup> / ''μ''<sub>tube</sub>}}. Since the length of the tube is proportional to the degree of polymerization, and μ<sub>tube</sub> is inversely proportional to the degree of polymerization, we observe that {{math|''τ'' ∝ (''DP''<sub>''n''</sub>)<sup>3</sup>}} (and so {{math|''τ'' ∝ ''M''<sup>3</sup>}}).

From the preceding analysis, we see that molecular mass has a very strong effect on relaxation time in entangled polymer systems. Indeed, this is significantly different from the untangled case, where relaxation time is observed to be proportional to molecular mass. This strong effect can be understood by recognizing that, as chain length increases, the number of tangles present will dramatically increase. These tangles serve to reduce chain mobility. The corresponding increase in relaxation time can result in [[Viscoelasticity|viscoelastic]] behavior, which is often observed in polymer melts. Note that 
the polymer's zero-shear [[viscosity]] gives an approximation of the actual observed dependency, {{math| ''τ'' ∝ ''M''<sup>3.4</sup>}};<ref name=Example2006b>{{cite book|last1=Berry |first1=G. C. |last2=Fox |first2=T. G. |chapter=The viscosity of polymers and their concentrated solutions |doi=10.1007/BFb0050985 |title=Fortschritte der Hochpolymeren-Forschung |publisher=Springer Berlin Heidelberg |series=Advances in Polymer Science |volume=5/3 |page=261 |year=1968 |isbn=978-3-540-04032-3}}</ref> this relaxation time has nothing to do with the reptation relaxation time.

== Models ==

[[File:Reptation- blob model.svg|thumb|right|The ''blob'' model, explaining the entanglement of long polymer chains.]]
[[File:Reptation Theory.svg|thumb|The tube model, explaining the basically one-dimensional mobility of long polymer chains.]]

Entangled polymers are characterized with effective internal scale, commonly known as ''the length of macromolecule between adjacent entanglements'' <math>M_\text{e}</math>.

Entanglements with other polymer chains restrict polymer chain motion to a thin virtual ''tube'' passing through the restrictions.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Edwards |first1=S. F. |doi=10.1088/0370-1328/92/1/303 |title=The statistical mechanics of polymerized material |journal=Proceedings of the Physical Society |volume=92 |issue=1 |pages=9–16 |year=1967 |bibcode=1967PPS....92....9E }}</ref> Without breaking polymer chains to allow the restricted chain to pass through it, the chain must be pulled or flow through the restrictions. The mechanism for movement of the chain through these restrictions is called reptation.

In the blob model,<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Duhamel |first1=J. |last2=Yekta |first2=A. |last3=Winnik |first3=M. A. |last4=Jao |first4=T. C. |last5=Mishra |first5=M. K. |last6=Rubin |first6=I. D. |doi=10.1021/j100153a046 |title=A blob model to study polymer chain dynamics in solution |journal=The Journal of Physical Chemistry |volume=97 |issue=51 |page=13708 |year=1993}}</ref> the polymer chain is made up of <math>n</math> [[Kuhn length]]s of individual length <math>l</math>. The chain is assumed to form blobs between each entanglement, containing <math>n_\text{e}</math> Kuhn length segments in each. The mathematics of random walks can show that the average end-to-end distance of a section of a polymer chain, made up of <math>n_\text{e}</math> Kuhn lengths is <math>d=l \sqrt{n_\text{e}}</math>. Therefore if there are <math>n</math> total Kuhn lengths, and <math>A</math> blobs on a particular chain:
: <math>A = \dfrac{n}{n_\text{e}}</math>

The total end-to-end length of the restricted chain <math>L</math> is then:
: <math>L = Ad = \dfrac{nl\sqrt{n_\text{e}}}{n_\text{e}} = \dfrac{nl}{\sqrt{n_\text{e}}}</math>

This is the average length a polymer molecule must diffuse to escape from its particular tube, and so the characteristic time for this to happen can be calculated using diffusive equations. A classical derivation gives the reptation time <math>t</math>:
: <math>t = \dfrac{l^2 n^3 \mu}{n_\text{e} k T}</math>
where <math>\mu</math> is the coefficient of friction on a particular polymer chain, <math>k</math> is the [[Boltzmann constant]], and <math>T</math> is the absolute temperature.

The linear macromolecules reptate if the length of macromolecule <math>M</math> is bigger than the critical entanglement molecular weight <math>M_\text{c}</math>. <math>M_\text{c}</math> is 1.4 to 3.5 times <math>M_\text{e}</math>.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Fetters |first1=LJ |last2=Lohse |first2=DJ |last3=Colby |first3=RH |editor1-last=Mark |editor1-first=James E |title=Chain Dimensions and Entanglement Spacings in "Physical properties of polymers handbook" |date=2007 |publisher=Springer New York |location=New York |isbn=978-0-387-69002-5 |page=448 |edition=2nd |chapter=25.3}}</ref> There is no reptation motion for polymers with <math>M < M_\text{c}</math>, so that the point <math>M_\text{c}</math> is a point of dynamic [[phase transition]].

Due to the reptation motion the coefficient of self-diffusion and conformational relaxation times of macromolecules depend on the length of macromolecule as <math>M^{-2}</math> and <math>M^3</math>, correspondingly.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Pokrovskii |first1=V. N. |doi=10.1016/j.physa.2005.10.028 |title=A justification of the reptation-tube dynamics of a linear macromolecule in the mesoscopic approach |journal=Physica A: Statistical Mechanics and Its Applications |volume=366 |pages=88–106|year=2006 |bibcode=2006PhyA..366...88P }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Pokrovskii |first1=V. N. |title=Reptation and diffusive modes of motion of linear macromolecules |doi=10.1134/S1063776108030205 |journal=Journal of Experimental and Theoretical Physics |volume=106 |issue=3 |pages=604–607 |year=2008 |bibcode=2008JETP..106..604P|s2cid=121054836 }}</ref> 
The conditions of existence of reptation in the thermal motion of macromolecules of complex architecture (macromolecules in the form of branch, star, comb and others) have not been established yet.

The dynamics of shorter chains or of long chains at short times is usually described by the [[Rouse model]].
